In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
pDC play an important role in the immune control of herpes virus infections in vivo.

pDC are not infected by HSV-1, but that pDC are recruited to the site of recurrent HSV-1 infection and may contribute to the control of the virus by secreting IFNs and stimulating virus-specific T-cell responses.
pDC are present at early and late time points in recurrent HSV lesions and that they may be important in the control of viral replication and in the stimulation of T cell immunity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
pDC play a role in HSV infection, but not as a target of infection.
pDC are not infected in vivo but are able to respond to HSV infection by producing interferon and by interacting with T cells and NK cells.

pDC are not only a component of the innate response to HSV infection in vitro but also are recruited to the skin during recurrent HSV infection in vivo, where they may play an important role in the control of viral replication and in the stimulation of the adaptive immune response.
The main takeaway from our work is that

plasmacytoid DC are not susceptible to HSV infection in vitro, but they are able to infiltrate the skin during HSV infection and they are activated in the skin by the infection, and that they are able to stimulate virus specific T cell proliferation in vitro.
pDC are not only important in innate immunity but may also be involved in the regulation of adaptive immunity.
